messages:
Raj (AcmeCorp): Hey team — hitting a ton of 429s and some connection timeouts from our private gateway after a marketing email blast. We're on the Private deployment (VPC) with a customer-managed gateway + nginx ingress. 429s start ~10s after burst, then latency spikes to 3-7s for other requests. Any quick triage advice?

Maya (Support): Sorry you're hitting this, Raj. A couple quick Qs: are you using the Redwood gateway image (vendor-managed) or a fully custom gateway in your k8s? Also, are the 429s token-based (API key) or IP-based? Any chance you can paste a short log snippet showing the 429s?

Raj (AcmeCorp): We're running the customer-managed gateway (we forked the gateway image to add our auth hook). 429s look API-key level. Sample from our gateway logs:

```
[2026-03-14T15:10:33Z] request_id=abc123 method=POST path=/v1/chat completion latency=210ms status=200 key=proj-x
[2026-03-14T15:10:34Z] request_id=abc124 method=POST path=/v1/chat completion latency=5ms status=429 key=proj-x reason=quota_exceeded
[2026-03-14T15:10:34Z] request_id=abc125 method=POST path=/v1/chat completion latency=3200ms status=504 key=proj-x
```

We have an nginx ingress with these annotations: 

```
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "200"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "400"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-burst-multiplier: "1"
```

Billing shows the tokens are still being charged for the 504s which is confusing.

Lena (Solutions Eng): Thanks — couple thoughts off the bat: (1) If you forked the gateway image and inserted an auth hook that calls back to your auth service synchronously, the auth check could be the bottleneck (adds latency and backpressure), (2) nginx RPS limits + small burst can queue upstream requests which then hit Redwood's token/accounting layer and still consume tokens even if upstream times out.

Can you reproduce locally with a short load test? If so, run something like:

```
# small reproducer
hey -n 2000 -c 200 -z 10s https://your-gateway.example.com/v1/chat -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -d '{"input":"hello"}'
```

That should show if the ingress is the first choke. Also paste your gateway config for timeouts (proxy_read_timeout/proxy_connect_timeout).

Sam (SRE): Two things to check server-side: (A) whether your gateway is sending X-Request-ID and X-Forwarded-For correctly — without that token mapping Redwood may treat concurrent retries as separate billable requests, (B) whether your KRATE limiter is configured for token-bucket semantics or leaky-bucket. If it's leaky-bucket with low burst, you'll see hard 429s during bursts.

Raj (AcmeCorp): Reproducer above returns a quick spike of 429s and then long tail 504s. Our gateway timeouts: proxy_read_timeout 60s, proxy_connect_timeout 5s. We set keepalive to 32. We do set X-Request-ID but our auth hook overwrites some headers. Example of our nginx location block:

```
location /v1/ {
  proxy_pass http://redwood-upstream;
  proxy_set_header X-Original-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
  proxy_read_timeout 60s;
  proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
  proxy_buffering on;
}
```

Maya (Support): Two immediate mitigations to try that often help: (1) increase the ingress burst allowance (so the upstream can accept short spikes without queuing all requests into your auth hook), and (2) make the auth hook async/cached for token validation so it returns quickly for repeat keys. Example nginx annotation tweak: `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "200"` and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-burst-multiplier: "3"`.

Also, set a short upstream timeout so requests that the gateway can't satisfy quickly fail fast and avoid charging tokens when upstream drops. For example, set `proxy_read_timeout: 10s` for the chat route while you stabilize.

Lena (Solutions Eng): On the Redwood side we recommend configuring a token-bucket style rate limiter for API keys with a burst that's >= typical email-blast concurrency. For example:

```
# recommended policy (pseudoconfig)
rate_limit {
  type: token_bucket
  tokens_per_sec: 100
  burst: 300
  scope: api_key
}
```

That lets short spikes of ~300 requests through without immediately 429-ing, then smooths to 100r/s. If your total per-key steady-state is lower, lower tokens_per_sec but keep burst high enough to avoid backpressure.

Sam (SRE): Additional K8s-level changes that have helped other customers:
- Use multiple gateway replicas and set `sessionAffinity: None` so bursts get spread.
- Increase envoy/nginx worker_connections and keepalives to avoid connection churn.
- Add an intermediate short in-memory auth cache (TTL 30s) keyed by API key or token fingerprint — reduces auth hook latency massively.

Raj (AcmeCorp): Quick question about billing: tokens still being charged for the 504s — is that expected? We're seeing accounts charged for requests that ultimately timed out upstream.

Maya (Support): Short answer: yes, billing is tied to tokens that were consumed by the model generation even if the gateway timed out before sending the full response. If you want to avoid token spend on requests that are likely to be dropped, use a pre-authorization check or apply gateway-side sampling/queue accept logic so heavy requests are rejected before being forwarded to Redwood. We'll open a billing investigation for cases that look like a platform bug, but in bursts it's usually because the request made it to model execution.

Lena (Solutions Eng): Repro steps to verify cause and mitigation (suggested runbook):
1) Instrument request path: enable debug logs in gateway and add a header `X-Client-Recv-Time` at entry and `X-Model-Started-Time` when Redwood receives it (if you can instrument).
2) Run the `hey` load test hitting the gateway with and without the auth hook to compare latency and 429 patterns.
3) Apply a conservative ingress change first: `limit-rps: 200`, `limit-burst-multiplier: 3`, `proxy_read_timeout: 10s` and watch error rate and billing.
4) If still problematic, migrate token validation to Redis-based shared cache in front of auth hook.

Raj (AcmeCorp): We're going to try the ingress changes now. Pushing a config update.

deploy-bot: Deployment started for ingress-configs/marketing-blast (sha: abcdef)
deploy-bot: Deployment succeeded — rollout complete (3 pods updated)

Raj (AcmeCorp): After changing to limit-rps 200 and burst-multiplier 3 + proxy_read_timeout 10s we see much fewer 504 tails. 429s still occur briefly but overall latency is stable. Billing still shows some spike at 15:10 when the blast was highest.

Maya (Support): Good progress. Follow-ups we should do together: (1) share request IDs around the spike time so Support can correlate with Redwood logs, (2) consider adding a per-route pre-accept policy: accept probability based on current queue depth to avoid sending too many requests to model execution, (3) we can provision a canary dedicated pool for high-volume keys if you expect repeated blasts — that avoids noisy-neighbor throttling.

Sam (SRE): One final tip — if you run the gateway inside k8s and rely on nginx ingress limits, be mindful that limit-rps is per-ingress-controller instance. When you autoscale controllers, effective global limits change unless you use a centralized rate-limiter (Envoy + rate-limit service or Redis-backed limiter). If you want deterministic global quotas, move to a centralized rate-limiter or configure the controller with a global shared store.

Raj (AcmeCorp): Thanks everyone — we'll implement the shared auth cache and look into centralized rate limit service. We'll also send a batch of request_ids for the peak window to Support for correlation. Appreciate the quick help. :thumbsup:

Maya (Support): Thanks Raj — please send the request IDs and we'll correlate and open a billing ticket if we find evidence of platform-side double-charge. Keeping this thread open until you confirm the shared cache rollout.

Sam (SRE): Leaving one note in case others hit this: quick nginx config snippet that helped one customer (use with caution):

```
# nginx conf fragment
limit_conn_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=addr:10m;
limit_conn addr 500;
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=req:50m rate=100r/s;
limit_req zone=req burst=400 nodelay;
proxy_read_timeout 10s;
proxy_send_timeout 10s;
```

This makes the ingress do a lot of the heavy lifting and fail fast before the auth/model path.

deploy-bot: Notifying monitoring: alert-suppression window applied for marketing-blast-2026-03-14

Raj (AcmeCorp): Confirmed — shared cache rolled out, early tests show much lower auth latency. We'll monitor billing and send request_ids if we still see anomalies. Thanks all.

Maya (Support): Great — marking as triaged for now. Reopen if billing anomalies persist or if you see any coord issues with dedicated pools.
